I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians want to change their government.

Polls taken throughout the country never fail to show that the Liberal party enjoys more prestige and popularity than any other party in Canada. The reason for this is that the government, under the leadership of Mr. St. Laurent, is worthy of the national approval. Some will try to stir prejudices, talk of scandals, magnify minor incidents, but they will be careful not to stress that under the St. Laurent administration, Canada has stood up before the world as one of the most prosperous nations, that our social legislation is one of the best, that the nation is expanding from month to month, that peace prevails in our country and that Canada is advancing toward accomplishments which other countries look at with envious eyes.

National defence imposes upon us a burden which is obvious to everyone. Mr. Speaker, after hearing the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on February 19 last and after having studied it thoroughly, I deemed it my duty to visit my constituency in order to find out the opinion of the electorate and their appreciation of the budget.
I might say that the workers and the farmers of my constituency have reacted to the budget in the most favourable and satisfactory manner, even though they expected a more substantial cut. The ideal would probably have been to obtain straight exemptions, but the international situation must be taken into consideration, as well as the numerous pieces of social legislation which the Liberal government has granted to the population of our country.
A glance at the statements appearing in the foreign press show that the feat performed by the Minister of Finance is considered as truly stupendous, not to say miraculous, whatever the member for Labelle (Mr. Courtemanche) may say to the contrary. One thing is sure, it is that the last budget reached all classes of society and resulted in a general tax reduction.
I shall not undertake to list the numerous exemptions which the Canadian people enjoy. It is sufficient for me to say that the tax rates have returned to the normal levels of 1949 and that in the last two budgets the Minister of Finance has reduced taxes by over $513 million. Obviously, this is frowned upon by the opposition groups whose criticisms are rank contradictions when the various statements are considered.
Some claim it is a pre-election budget which favours the low income groups, that is the majority of taxpayers. That was the first reaction of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell); others contend that it is a rich man's budget; others still say that it is a budget which favours corporations.
I wish to discuss the matter in order to prove that no one was overlooked in this budget. For this purpose, may I quote statistics in connection with my own constituency in order to show the benefits provided by the budget.
I have here a newspaper which reported last Thursday that in my district alone, that is to say in La Mauricie, more than 4,000 tons of newsprint were shipped every day over one railway line. As that newsprint

The Budget-Mr. Rochefort sells for $125 a ton, we may say that the value of such production exceeds $500,000 a day. In my home constituency, at Cap de la Madeleine and Three Rivers, 2,500 tons of newsprint are produced every day, which represents a value of more than $300,000, and the 2,500 men who find employment in that industry draw more than $100,000 a day in wages.
At Cap de la Madeleine, in 1950, out of 5,941 wage earners, there were only 2,300 taxpayers. That is to say that with 3,641 people paying no tax, 60 per cent of the workers, men and women, in that town were not taxable and, in fact, did not pay tax. The 2,300 taxpayers paid $320,000 on a reported income of $6,436,000, in other words $1 for each $20 earned. Since then the government removed the 20 per cent surtax for national defence; also the workers had their wages increased in 1952 by 12 per cent. I have here a newspaper excerpt, announcing an increase of 10 per cent for employees of the paper mills in my constituency, starting March 1, 1953 and of 6 cents an hour retroactive to May 1952. To this must be added the latest tax reduction of 11 per cent, effective July 1, 1953.
The paper mill workers of my constituency earn between $60 and $150 a week. Once they have deducted their personal and their dependents' allowances, contributions to charitable organizations, medical or hospital expenses, most of them, that is approximately 60 per cent, pay no income tax whatever, the remainder paying a moderate amount, which has constantly been decreasing with every budget brought down lately.
Moreover the government having managed to check inflation, the cost of living has gone down 2 per cent. This decrease has brought, about a general fall in food and clothing prices. The same obtains in every industry in my constituency where the salary scale is everywhere 300 or 400 per cent higher than when the Tory party administered the affairs of this country during the 1930-35 period.
Compare the salaries earned today with those we have known during the hunger and misery stricken, debt-ridden period between 1930 and 1935, when this country was governed by the Conservative party.
I met this week a worker who supervises a paper machine; he earned $48 a month in 1932, because his mill was operating only two days a week; now, under a Liberal regime, this same worker earns $860 a month.

The man earns $4,000 a year more than the member for that county. Of course, he pays income tax, but he is glad to do so, because he has the salary required to pay it, while he was starving under the Conservatives. Today this worker has a bank account which increases every day, he owns his own house, his children are attending schools, he has a son at the university, he even has his own car; he knows now what well-being and comfort are, what it is to be well-off, while in the former days, under a Conservative regime, he knew but misery, starvation and debts.
Ask him, even if he now pays income tax, whether he would change his present status with that of the years 1930-1935. It is the same with all workers of the county of Champlain and, mind you, the salary scales have more than doubled in the course of the last few years in all these industries. And yet 60 per cent of all these workers pay no tax. How can you reduce the tax of the lower income bracket when it pays no tax at all?
The minimum salary paid since March 1 last in paper mills is $1.38 per hour and the maximum salary, $2.95 per hour, which amounts to nearly $24 a day. Working conditions are excellent. This worker enjoys three weeks' holidays with pay. He contributes to a pension fund. In case of illness in hospital he and the members of his family are assured of special assistance. In the plant he is given free medical and nursing care. Go and ask this worker if he is willing to exchange the system of the present Liberal government for the system of direct relief tokens, of Murling shelters, of soup kitchens, an institution greatly favoured by the Conservative party when it was in power from 1930 to 1935.
In every one of the factories in my constituency, I would find the same working conditions, the same wages and the same good employer-employee relations.
In my riding there are three newsprint mills, three paper bag factories, one enormous paper foils factory, which plans to expand shortly, two abrasive manufacturing plants, about ten textile plants, a shoe factory, six glove factories, smelters and over forty private undertakings. All those plants are operating at full capacity. Salaries range from a minimum of 90 cents per hour to $2.
Here is real prosperity for which the Liberal government of this country is responsible. Its achievements have nothing to do with

petty quarrels arising from political patronage; its policy is not to enrich its friends or to fill the pork barrel.
At the beginning of the session, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) pointed out to the house that if the suggestions of the Leader of the Opposition and his lieutenants were to be implemented, taxes would double in this country. After listing the latest requests of the Conservative party, the Prime Minister said that it would be necessary to increase if not to double taxes in order to meet all the requests of the opposition. Moreover, he stated that the result would be a deficit of half a billion dollars a year. Their electors may well ask them if they have not diverted the federal mandate they have been entrusted with to serve their own purposes? I will simply ask them the following question: If the party they support were in power, would they try to take away the revenue of the country and turn it over to the provinces?
We have reason to question the good faith of their arguments and to consider their statements rather as a joke. We can ask ourselves whether these false autonomists are not, rather, seeking electoral funds to ensure their re-election in their own constituencies. Are these people really trying in this house to promote the interests of Quebec; we have every reason to doubt it.
The interests of our country and our province in particular are more secure in the hands of the present Prime Minister than in the hands of those people. The interests of this country are better protected by the Liberal party than by any other party. The fairness of the social legislation of the Liberal government proves it.
Let them show me in what way Quebec has been unfairly treated. Let them point out in what way the treatment meted out to our people was inferior to the treatment of the other provinces. Canada must be a political union of two great races, prepared by men of vision and tolerance, a union in which the two associates would preserve their essential character, their relationship, their language and their culture.
Is there any better or more sincere evidence than this, the statement of this country's leader? Here is another statement made by the Prime Minister, on October 28, 1952:
To my mind the Liberal party's aim must be to maintain this country's unity and security, as the home of a free people. The government must then, having ensured national security, concern itself mainly with the freedom and welfare of the individual and of the family.
Can there be greater evidence of faith, honour and honesty, of faithfulness to his own kindred than these words uttered by the Liberal leader who is at the head of government at the present time?

Mr. Speaker, despite all that has been said so far I should like to draw attention to a few points which in my opinion have not been sufficiently emphasized and which I believe are quite important. Opposition members have referred to this budget as an election budget. If it is an election budget then the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) deserves all our praise and commendation for resisting the temptation to hand out bribes to the masses in an election year. In fact the chief criticism that has been levelled at this budget is that it does nothing or very little for the little man who, as we know, controls the majority of the votes.
In my opinion the budget is realistic and straightforward. It follows a pattern which has been established in previous years. It takes into consideration prevailing conditions both at home and abroad. Double taxation has been abolished, and tax cuts have been spread among all groups of taxpayers in such a way as to strike a fair balance between direct and indirect taxation.
There has been no cut in expenditures, and this is in line with reality. The international situation will not permit any lessening of our defence effort. The wishes of the people, which are always the deciding factor in a democracy, demand that there should be no curtailment in our social security program. The needs of our public service are just as great as in previous years and the yearly increment in salaries necessitates an
The Budget-Mr. Carter annual increase in the cost of administration. Therefore no reduction in expenditures is possible.
My constituency is distinctive in that all my constituents are in the low income group. This particular group has been singled out for priority of consideration in all our previous budgets. Taxes have been eliminated from nearly all the necessities of life. For those who pay little or no income tax, very little more can be done. Yet this budget does grant them some benefits in the abolition of the stamp tax and the radio licence fee. Our fishermen will benefit from the abolition of taxes on marine motors and wire ropes, and also from the reduction of the tax on cigarettes.
In addition, this low income group will continue to receive benefits in the form of family allowances, old age pensions and other forms of social security included in the billion dollar program provided in this budget. In this way the wealth of the whole nation is distributed among all classes and groups so that the little man may enjoy a far greater share than he would otherwise receive.
The budget makes it clear that tax reductions have been made possible only because of the increase in our gross national product. This gross national product is simply the sum total of the wealth produced by all Canadians in all parts of Canada. Every fisherman, every farmer, every logger, every miner, every factory worker, every industrialist and every person who supplies essential services makes a contribution to it. The budget recognizes this fact, and we feel it is a wise policy to provide incentive and encouragement to every Canadian to keep on producing more and more because that is the only guarantee of further reduction of taxation in the future.
No human effort can be perfect. It is unreasonable to expect that this budget could be perfect in every detail. Like the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) I would like to have seen more reduction in the tax on pipe tobacco because most of my constituents are pipe smokers. Like the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) I would like to have seen blind pensions increased and the means test abolished. I would like to have seen the same done with respect to the war veterans allowance. I would like to have seen provision made for war widows, and those who are incapacitated.
But with so many items to be considered, human wisdom is simply not able to determine exactly how much consideration any one item deserves in comparison with every other item. Neither is it able to measure
2822	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Carter exactly where the line should be drawn between federal responsibility on the one hand and provincial and individual responsibility on the other. We cannot escape being our brother's keeper no matter how much we may wish to push that responsibility over on the federal government. We have travelled a long way already on that road, and now it is necessary to pause and see where the road is leading lest we eventually end up by making the federal government responsible for everything and everybody and with nobody else having any responsibility at all.
One important feature of the budget is the spotlight which it throws on the magnitude of the industrial potential and almost limitless natural resources which make Canada one of the most richly blessed nations on the face of the earth. This has brought to my mind two thoughts. One thought is the danger that we Canadians may take all this wealth and attendant prosperity for granted, the danger lest we adopt the attitude that we have a special right to all these blessings because of some merit in ourselves as compared with other peoples on the earth. The second thought is what a tremendous responsibility rests upon every single one of us to see that all this wealth is not used selfishly, merely to satisfy our own needs, but also to help take care of the needs of those nations less fortunate than ourselves.
Let us learn the lesson of the strategic and ideological use of wealth that Russia taught us in her trade agreement with Ceylon. We know how Russia, while the western nations dallied, took advantage of Ceylon's need for food and offered her rice at less than the world price in return for her rubber at more than the world price, and by so doing tied the whole economy of Ceylon to the communist world.
I have been wondering whether we might not consider if it is possible to do something along that line with our millions of bushels of surplus wheat and grain. We all know that a number of nations are suffering from a shortage of food, and it would be a fine thing if we could use our surplus food in such a strategic manner, not with any thought of national gain or advantage or with any ulterior motive, but simply out of genuine caring for people as people. I believe if we could do this the nations of the world, and particularly the nations of the east, would recognize something new in our democratic way of life and would be attracted to it.
Mr. Speaker, the budget does not permit very much room for criticism. Consequently opposition members have been forced to resort to charges of waste and extravagance, coupled with the inference that consequently

tax reductions are not as great as they should be. Well, that same argument could also be applied to strikes, to laziness, to indifference, to dishonest labour, to evasion of taxes, to illegal drawing of social benefits and to many other things. When producers are more concerned with keeping prices at a certain level than they are with meeting the needs of their fellow men, then they tend to produce only such quantities as they believe will keep prices at the highest possible level. That too tends to lessen the gross national product and consequently reduces the possibility of tax relief.
All this is only another way of saying that if there were no greed, no selfishness, no dishonesty in the world or in the nation there would be still greater production of wealth and a still greater share of tax relief. We hear a great deal about the greed and the selfishness of the big man, the big corporation. No one can deny that that is a terrible thing, and that it was in great measure responsible for bringing about conditions which gave birth to communism and enabled it to grow and thrive.
But I think we should point out to the little man that today he exercises just as great power as the big man, if not more. What industrialist or group of industrialists can tie up the whole economy of a country by stopping its transportation facilities? What group of magnates can strangle the trade of a nation by closing off its ports? What group of industrialists can undermine the whole economy of a nation by cutting off the supply of strategic materials like fuel and coal?"
The point is that power carries with it responsibility, no matter whether it is exercised by the big man or the little man; and I think the little man too must come to realize that his greed and selfishness, when mobilized and used as a force, can be just as great a danger and threat to the life and welfare of the nation as those of the vested interests.
Opposition members have referred to cost-plus and percentage-cost contracts as particular examples of waste and extravagance. But as the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) pointed out this afternoon, does not that too boil down to a question of individual honesty? If the individual contractors were absolutely honest what difference would it make whether they had a percentage-plus contract, a cost-plus contract or any other kind? I find it interesting to examine the proposals which our friends on the opposition side have put forth to solve this problem. They cry out for more controls, more checks, more guards, more laws, more legislation.

I was struck by a statement made by our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a few days ago when he was replying to a brief submitted by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. In referring to human rights he pointed out that no nation on the earth had more elaborately worded clauses about human rights in its constitution than did Soviet Russia. So the opposition cry out: Change the government, change the ministry; but will changing the government make individual contractors more honest-

For the greater part of the past six sessions, Mr. Speaker, I have been sitting back here in this kindergarten row. I have not done much talking, but I have done a great deal of listening. I have been trying to figure out just what is my responsibility as a member of this parliament. So, should any pressure group come to me and say: "Carter, we voted for you in the last election, now you have to do this for us- or else", it would be my duty to say to them: "Do you really want an honest government? Mr. Speaker, the budget proves that Canada is a great and growing country 

destined to wield great influence among the nations of the world. It is a story of the achievement of a free people in a free economy under a system of free enterprise. The Liberal party has always placed its main stress on freedom, and under the leadership of the Liberal party we have achieved a large measure of political and economic freedom. Mr. Speaker, I was interested in a remark made by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) when he commenced his address to the house yesterday. He said that during his early experience in this house he discovered that a good deal of the time during speech-making was spent in propaganda and, as a result, he resolved not to spend too much time making speeches in this chamber.
I agree with him that during this budget debate there has been considerable propaganda uttered that perhaps is more designed for consumption outside this house than by members in the chamber. However, I cannot agree with him that the same thing applies in every debate. Since I came to this house a relatively short time ago I have had the privilege of sitting in on some very significant discussions dealing with problems of extreme importance both to our internal economy and with regard to our external affairs.
I suppose it is inevitable that during the budget speech in a pre-election period the tenor of the discussion should take on something of an electioneering aspect. Indeed, as I sat and listened here that night almost three weeks ago when the minister delivered the budget address, I would say that the minister himself established the pace because primarily I believe the budget for this year was designed to appeal directly to the electorate. Since that time, as various members have discussed the subject, they have followed along on the same line.
During the discussion it seems that the press outside Canada has become most interested in affairs relating to the government of this country. We have had one hon. member after another make reference to the editorials appearing particularly in the press across the line with regard to the excellence of this government and the excellence of the budget that was presented to the house. I was most intrigued to discover that even the press in Ireland made some reference to the budget speech. I thought that reference perhaps was most suitable to the occasion, because the Irish are notable for having

kissed the blarney stone. A good many of the references from south of the line also showed a similar influence even though they did not come from Ireland itself.
I should like to mention a quotation that comes to my mind-it is a good Irish quotation-which runs something like this: The sweetest memories of life are the recollections of things forgotten. It seems to me that in the skilful manner in which the budget was presented there was, on the part of the minister, an attempt to have the Canadian people forget a great many things that have occurred during the past few years in this country.
There was a time when it was popular, particularly in the west, to refer to the C.C.F. as Liberals in a hurry; and as Canada moved toward the social welfare state as a result of the major disturbances of the depression it almost seemed as though that statement were true. But this time we have a budget that is back-tracking in a rather extreme fashion. There seems to be a swing back to what we might call free enterprise or, to use the phrase that is sometimes preferred, responsible enterprise. The new look that is supposed to have appeared on the faces of the members of the opposition during the delivery of the budget speech that night is, I think, nothing more or less than a look of incredulity because, among the many incredible things this government has done during the past 18 years, this was an extreme example of its flexibility and its ability to swing backward and forward in order to meet the demands of the situation.
Before proceeding to some of the aspects of the budget I want to quote from an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 17, 1951. I think this article expresses in a precise manner what the government is attempting to do as it moves backward and forward and changes complexion almost with the same dexterity as the chameleon. I once heard a story about the chameleon. As hon. members know, it is that little lizard which has the power to adapt itself to various colours and hues. A rather nasty trick was once played on the poor little creature by putting it on a Scotsman's plaid, and it burst as it attempted to adapt itself to the various colours. That just might happen in the case of a government that becomes too flexible with regard to its policies.
Incidentally, this article is entitled "The Collapse of the Opposition". I think it expresses the secret desire or the wishful thinking on the part of the government that that state of affairs was or is going to happen, namely that the opposition will collapse completely and that we shall move toward the
The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale one-party state where power in perpetuity would be carried on.

From the Winnipeg Free Press of May 17, 1951. It reads as follows:
The Liberal party, on the other hand, has achieved such an unchallenged sense of regnancy and success that it can afford to admit that the total disequilibrium of politics is a bad thing for the country, perhaps even for itself.
In a minor but significant fashion the present political calculations of this capital will be tested by four federal by-elections in June-two in Manitoba, one in Ontario and one on Prince Edward Island. It will surprise government and opposition alike if any of these seats-three Liberal, one Conservative-switch from one party to the other.
As it turned out, this prophecy was completely wrong. To go on a little bit further in the article, summing up the general discussion the writer says:
The Liberal party, in short, has found a way of occupying so fully the middle ground of politics, moving right or left as the occasion requires, that there is presently no adequate room for a successful opponent on either side. The government's pragmatism has become almost a science.
I would agree with that article, as we see the swing that has been indicated in the budget that was brought into the house just a few weeks ago.
As we have engaged in pre-electioneering discussion, the keynote from the government benches has been to make an appeal on the basis of the prevailing wave of prosperity in Canada. This prosperity has been emphasized particularly by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who the other day brought down statistics in order to make a comparison and to contrast the buoyancy of today with the stagnation of the depression period. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has also made reference many times to this prevailing high level of prosperity; and again, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) dwelt upon it at length in his remarks.
I first became politically aware during the latter thirties, and if I may speak on a personal note I should like to do so. Usually the depression is emphasized as covering the years 1930 to 1935. As soon as the Liberals returned to office the depression was supposed to have miraculously withered away. But I was quite politically aware as a young chap in 1937, and I do not recall that things were unusually buoyant during that year. As a matter of fact I, along with several other graduates fresh from college in 1937, had absolutely no job opportunities available. Hundreds of our young men, myself included, were obliged to look for work in any direction in which they could possibly find it. I did not discover in 1937 that our economy

The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale was unduly buoyant. In fact it was the continuing economic distress that turned my thinking toward some form of social work.
I remember that as late as the year 1939-
I was working in the city of Montreal-I was discussing this problem with some knights of the road who had been on the go for almost ten years, travelling up and down the country, as so many of our young men did during the decade of the thirties. They were discussing the period when relief camps had been provided for unemployed men.

Yes; and those were abruptly done away with, as I recall it, after the Liberals returned to power. This chap commenting said: "Mr. Bennett gave us relief camps at least, but all that the Liberals gave us was the highways to pound". He had been pounding them across the country for quite a considerable period of time. Therefore, from a personal recollection of those events, I do not think there was a miraculous recovery, a miraculous return to prosperous conditions overnight, as is sometimes suggested by members from the government side of this chamber.
I was very interested, Mr. Speaker, in the speech made by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) this afternoon in which he tried to deal in some detail with this situation. It is high time someone did take it upon himself to be intellectually honest on this matter. With respect to many speeches that have been made on the subject, there tends to be intellectual dishonesty in this house. I do not think there is any more glaring example of intellectual dishonesty than the tendency, by subtle propaganda, to insinuate that the depression was caused by any particular group; or, on the other hand, that the prevailing prosperity today is on account of the machinations of any particular group that might be in office. This point must be emphasized over and over again if we are to have a responsible and enlightened attitude on the part of the electorate in this country.
I do not need to emphasize it; it should be almost obvious enough to be self-explanatory. If I had time, or if the occasion warranted it, I could go on and mention positive contributions that have been made by the Conservative party when we have had periods of power in this country. Of course everyone admits that the same could be said of the Liberals when they have enjoyed periods of power. The Conservative party, one of the historical political parties of this country, in fact the party that was largely responsible for initiating confederation, is steeped in the traditions of this country. It

has been the champion of the rights of parliament and of the people of Canada down through the years. According to that very interesting book "The Incredible Canadian", the fact that the Conservatives won the 1930 election was later recognized by the late prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, as the most fortunate thing that had ever happened to his party. Had the reverse situation prevailed, then the political story of Canada since that time would have been much different from what it has actually been.
It was encouraging to me-and this represents one of the occasions when discussion in this house reached a relatively high level -to hear references made from all sides of the house to the work of Sir Robert Borden during world war I, in connection with the provision of a sum of money to have his statue erected on parliament hill. Without any political consideration entering into the discussion the true stature of the man was measured, and even though he belonged to a party other than that in office at the moment he was given credit for having brought Canada a long step forward under his leadership toward the national autonomy within the framework of the British commonwealth of nations that has been completely established today.
Even during the depression some creditable efforts were made. I need only mention the imperial conference, the establishment of the central bank and others. I have been interested on several occasions to hear the leader of the C.C.F. party refer in complimentary tones to some of the policies that Mr. Bennett tried to bring forward under the new deal in an attempt to grapple with the extremely difficult economic situation that prevailed in the early thirties as well as in the late thirties. The whole country was slow to move toward the emergency legislation necessary to cope with an almost complete collapse of our economy, and that applied to other countries in the western world as well. In fact some of the countries of Europe, as we only too well know, were not as successful in grappling with the problems as we were, and dictatorship, tyranny and general political and economic confusion resulted. Therefore in making this unfair comparison-and it seems to be one of the chief appeals to the people of Canada at this time-contrasting prevailing prosperity with so-called Tory depression, I think we have a glaring example of intellectual dishonesty.
Associated with this same technique we have the constant reference to the tariff issue. During the twenties the tariff issue proved very helpful in pitting the east against the west, and thus making it possible for

the Liberal party to hold power on the basis of dividing and conquering.

The hon. member for Dauphin has made reference to this so-called Tory protectionism. I can quite understand his opinion because he was closely associated with the Progressive movement back in the early twenties, and it was the absorption of the Progressives into the Liberal party during that period, after the Progressives had sent some 65 or 66 agrarian representatives to this house, that forced the Liberal group at least to give lip service to the principle of free trade. The agrarian reformers were ardent free traders.
The old struggle, the old attitude, the old conflict of the east versus the west, the suspicion of the west toward the east, still persists on the prairies. During the twenties it crystallized into the protection versus free trade issue. It was a red herring issue then, if we examine it to its source, and it is even more of a red herring today than it was during the twenties.
I was reading in the report on the South Saskatchewan dam at page 72, where it refers to the policy of national development which was first initiated by John A. Macdonald, and has been carried forth by successive governments since that day. The policy included the construction of the transcontinental railway and the opening of the west to settlement. In reference to the Liberal contribution to that policy after 1896 this report says:
Liberal governments which followed in power after 1896-
That is which followed Conservative governments.
-maintained the protective system with only minor modifications in the direction of imperial preference. The protective system has been the national policy to Canadians to the present day.
That is so, with minor variations and flexibility. And let me quote further from a definitive statement on the subject by Robert MacGregor Dawson in his book "The Government of Canada". This is one of the few text books on the subject of Canadian government. At page 502, referring to the platforms or policies of Liberal and Conservative governments he says:
The nearest approach to a constant policy has been furnished by the stand of each party on the protective tariff. The more extreme Liberal tendencies towards free trade, as noted above, were already toned down before the party victory of 1896; but the introduction of the imperial preference indicated that Liberal principles had not been entirely forsaken. The party, however, then rested on its achievement and retained a tariff which was unmistakably protectionist in character until the

The Budget-Mr. Dinsdale government brought down its proposals for reciprocity with the United States in 1911. It was an ironical turn of events that when the Liberals at last made a sincere attempt to carry one of their neglected principles into practice they sustained defeat. In 1921, when they returned to power, they reduced the tariff in piecemeal fashion over a number of years; but it would be an exaggeration to state that this resulted in anything more than a moderate tariff which never lost sight of its protective function. Moreover, while there may be a strong likelihood, there is no assurance that the Liberals at this time would, if left to themselves, have gone even as far as they did, for their position in parliament was so uncertain that they were by no means free to do as they pleased. They lacked a genuine majority and were being kept in office by Progressive support, and the tariff reductions were moves in a long courtship which was designed to soften the heart of the western free-trading farmers.
Then, if I might quote further, I would turn to Hansard for 1935 where, at page 1962, Mr. Rhodes, speaking in the budget debate and referring to this old tariff bogey, had this to say:
In 1933, at the world economic conference the delegates from Canada strongly advocated the general adoption of a policy of removing the excessive restrictions which were strangling world trade, and the responsibility for the failure to adopt it must rest elsewhere. Since that time we have been carrying on negotiations with various individual countries some of which have been completed, others are still in progress. During the last few days you have been made acquainted with the comprehensive trade agreement which has been concluded with France and which, it may be said, for the first time places our trade relations with that country on an entirely satisfactory basis. Negotiations have been practically completed with Poland for a treaty which will enable Canadian trade to be carried on satisfactorily with that growingly important country from which, in the absence of a treaty, our products have been hitherto almost entirely excluded.
During recent months, an opportunity has presented itself for the first time since this government assumed office to enter into negotiations with a view to effecting a trade agreement with the United States of America.
Those negotiations, as I recall, had been restricted or prevented by the existence of the Hawley-Smoot tariff in the United States. It was the beginning of negotiations referred to in the speech by Mr. Rhodes that led the way to the establishment of an agreement to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell) and the hon. member for Dauphin. Those preliminary negotiations, as Mr. Rhodes indicated, were undertaken by a Conservative administration, and were only finalized after the election to office of a Liberal government in 1935.
It is a phony issue. It is a red herring issue. It is designed to appeal primarily to the west; and to bring it up in this day and age as a significant plank in a party platform indicates a failure to understand the changes which have taken place in the west since

Today the west is driving very strenuously and enthusiastically toward a diversified economy, and they will not be deterred from their purpose by the resurrection from the dead of an issue which no longer has any appeal among prairie farmers.
We now know that if we are going to cope with some of the tremendous economic problems which are facing us on the prairies, problems which have been brought into focus within recent days by the loss of prairie parliamentary representation in the house, when two of the prairie provinces, namely Manitoba and Saskatchewan, have lost membership in the house because of their relative decline in population-I say that if we are to cope with these problems we realize that we must diversify our economy. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall continue this debate.

At ten, o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, March 11, 1953
